children: By Isabella Simonetti and Meridith McGraw
President Trump's effort to ban three news outlets from the White House escalated tensions between the president and the journalists who cover him.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico sued to overturn the ban and restore their journalists' press credentials, and a federal judge ruled early Thursday that the administration had to temporarily lift the ban.

After the White House removed CNN from a planned assignment to cover Trump's trip to New York City earlier this week, the major television networks collectively agreed to suspend some video coverage of the president. The TV pool was restored Friday.

Trump has rebuffed suggestions that his actions threaten the free press: "The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish," he wrote Monday on Truth Social. "It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America."
Here's how the White House press pool works.
What is the press pool?

The White House press pool is a rotation of reporters, videographers, photographers and technicians who cover the president when he travels or when he conducts events in spaces that are too small for the entire press corps.
The pool typically includes more than a dozen journalists that send written reports, audio, video and photos to thousands of news outlets, who then distribute the information to people worldwide.
How does it work?

The television pool, a subset of the broader pool of journalists covering the president, includes ABC News, CBS News, CNN, Fox News and NBC News. The networks take turns serving as the primary television pooler each day. Fox News parent Fox Corp. and The Wall Street Journal's parent News Corp share common ownership.

There is also a separate daily print reporter and a radio reporter, who each distribute reporting on the president's activities to news outlets. Print-pool reports are circulated widely by the White House press office. The Journal is part of the print pool.
A typical pool day at the White House can include covering several events in the Oval Office or other parts of the White House, and last many hours.

For out-of-town trips, an even smaller group of journalists travels with the president and goes in Trump's motorcade and on Air Force One. Their job is to report on the president's movements and public statements, and to ask questions on behalf of the entire press corps. Foreign-pool assignments can last for days. The Journal was the print pooler during Trump's recent weekend trip to Ireland.
Who pays the pool travel expenses?
The cost of the travel is paid by the news organizations.
What is new?

The major television networks suspended the television-pool rotation after CNN was removed from the New York assignment earlier in the week. Dozens of news organizations filed a court brief supporting the banned outlets, and some said they wouldn't use pool photographs or audio in solidarity until CNN was let back into the rotation.
The White House continued to stream events live on its website and YouTube channel.

Early Thursday morning, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly in Washington, D.C., ordered a temporary pause on the ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters as litigation proceeded. He said the removal of reporters' press badges was likely done without "constitutionally adequate due process."
Reporters for the three news outlets regained their White House access by around midday on Thursday, and the TV pool resumed coverage Friday morning.
How does the attempted ban fit into the White House's other media-access actions?

The Trump administration has exercised more control over traditional White House media coverage. The White House said last year that it would determine which news organizations and reporters can be part of the press pool. It took much of that responsibility over from the White House Correspondents' Association, a nonpartisan media group. The White House also took over the seating chart for the press briefing room, adding a "new media" seat.

Meanwhile, the White House introduced other direct-to-consumer options including a page on its website with links to selected articles about Trump's policies, agenda actions and positive polling results.
